Secondary home sales volume unexpectedly rebounded 17% y-y in March (range from - 25% to +90%)   in terms of real-time transactions in the 25 major cities we track (vs. +1% yy in 2M26). The rebound continued into April, with   faster growth of 30% y-y (range from - 15% to +74%) on a low base, pushing YTD growth to 14% y-y in 4M26 (range from -22% to +61%). This strong performance has led to mild m-m home price increases in Shanghai and Beijing (cumulatively up 1-2% in March to April), and a softer m-m home price decline in a number of Tier 2 cities.

Chinese New Year (CNY) in mid-February this year was about three weeks later than that in 2025. Historically, home sales are muted during CNY holidays, and gradually recover sequentially as people return to work. This year, work resumption time coincided with the traditional high home sales season in March. If we compare on a CNY-adjusted basis, the cumulative growth of secondary home sales would be much milder at 18% y-y post CNY.

More importantly, compared on a cumulative basis, we note that secondary home sales volumes significantly underperformed in 4Q25 (-28% y-y on average) amid an accelerated home price drop in the quarter, but had notably narrowed the y-y decline in March and April. We attribute this fast catch-up partially to policy easing (e.g., Beijing and Shanghai relaxed their home purchase restrictions in late December and late February, respectively), and partially to the release of pent-up demand amid less-bearish home-buyer sentiment post the removal of negative views about the housing market in social media (conducted in November-December 2025).

Indeed, high-frequency data appear supportive of our deceleration view, with MTD secondary real-time home sales volume softening to +24% y-y by May 12. Other than cities with a recent policy boost, we see fast cooling in most of the cities we track, especially in Tier 2 cities, including Beijing, +11% y-y versus +30% in April; Zhuhai, -38% versus +45%; Wuxi, +41% versus +70%; Dongguan, +52% versus +74%; Dalian, +24% versus +44%; Tianjin, +11% versus +26%; Nanchang, +43% versus +57%; Shenyang, +15% versus +27%; Wuhan, +28% versus +39%; Nanjing, +16% versus +26%; Xi'an, +38% versus +46%; and Chengdu, +9% versus +15%.

In contrast to the strong rebound in secondary home sales, the primary market witnessed a much weaker performance, and have been lagging secondary market for more than three months. According to CREIS data, the primary home sales in the 25 major cities we track decreased 16% y-y in March, and increased only 4% y-y in April despite the low base. Combining the primary and secondary sales together, the total transaction volume in these cities increased 8% y-y in March (ranging from -28% to +67%) and 23% y-y in April (ranging from -10% to +73%).

- Hiked transactions of small lump-sum housing: According to Bingshan data, housing with >20 years age, and with a small lump-sum (e.g., less than Rmb5mn in Beijing/Shanghai/Shenzhen, less than Rmb3mn in Hangzhou/Chengdu/Xiamen) accounted for >40% and >80% of the secondary transactions in these major cities in April, respectively. In addition, the housing lump-sum index has been dropping faster than the home price index since 2025, and has continued to fall faster in 4M26 (-3.3% vs. -1.6% in 42 cities), indicating an enlarging contribution of small lump-sum housing in total transactions.

On the other hand, we expect primary home sales volume to remain negative y-y in the coming quarters due to reduced saleable resources at developers, although a favorable base may narrow the YTD decline to high-single-digit %, versus -13.1% y-y in 3M26. Adding primary and secondary sales together, full-year home sales volume could be largely flat yy in volume terms, which is 3-4 ppt better than our previous forecast.

As these properties are generally located in decent locations (e.g., with good community facilities and school catchments), but have experienced larger-thanmarket home price declines in the past few years due to below-average building quality, the rental yield of these housing has exceeded the mortgage rate of loans from the Housing Provident Fund (HPF). For example, the rental yield of this old/ small lump-sum housing in Beijing and Shanghai could offer a 3%+ rental yield, which is higher than the HPF mortgage loan rate of 2.6%. Thus, they are appealing to first-home buyers, such as migrant workers who are now qualified for home purchases after the recent relaxation of home purchase restrictions, and higher HPF loan caps. In contrast, primary homes in comparable locations generally have a larger unit size and, thus, a larger lump-sum that mainly targets buyers for home upgrades.

Bingshan data show that housing rental rates in 76 major cities have cumulatively dropped 15% since July 2021 amid the housing downtrend, including -3.1% y-y in 2022, -1.8% in 2023, -4.9% in 2024, and -3.8% in 2025. Compared with low-tier cities, which have minimal rental demand, high-tier cities have experienced an even deeper pullback, including -25% in Hangzhou and Nanjing, -23% in Zhengzhou, -20% in Wuhan, -17% in Chengdu, and -16% in Shanghai and Shenzhen. Given that home prices have retreated much faster over the period, with a cumulative decline of >40%, the average rental yield in these cities has improved to 2.70% in April 2026, versus 2.01% before the correction. This includes 2.02% in Beijing, versus 1.62%; 1.95% in Shanghai, versus 1.56%; 1.79% in Shenzhen, versus 1.42%; and 2.05% in Guangzhou, versus 1.56%.

CRIC data show that primary inventory in 70 major cities reached record-high levels across all city tiers at 32 months in March 2026, including 23 months in Tier 1 cities, 30 months in Tier 2 cities, and 42 months in Tier 3 cities, versus historical averages of 14, 15, and 18 months, respectively. This is consistent with our estimate that the national primary inventory level was ~40 months in 2025, given that low-tier cities tend to have more challenging oversupply issues.

CRIC data show that primary inventory in 70 major cities reached record-high levels across all city tiers at 32 months in March 2026, including 23 months in Tier 1 cities, 30 months in Tier 2 cities, and 42 months in Tier 3 cities, versus historical averages of 14, 15, and 18 months, respectively. This is consistent with our estimate that the national primary inventory level was ~40 months in 2025, given that low-tier cities tend to have more challenging oversupply issues.

The digestion of primary inventory has been much slower than the market expected, cumulatively falling ~25% from the 2020 peak in absolute terms in these 70 cities, despite national land sales volume having cumulatively dropped >65% over the period to 473mn sqm in 2025, equivalent to 35% below the primary residential sales volume of 733mn sqm in the year. We attribute the slow digestion partially to weak sales of developers' old inventory, and partially to the market shift toward secondary home sales due to more competitive pricing.

Sales durability is a concern: While the recent strong secondary sales rebound may suggest the worst has passed in select high-tier cities,   limited improvement in macro and housing indicators, divergent trends between new and secondary homes, and still-fragile home-buyer sentiment lead us to doubt the sustainability of the rebound, which will hinge on replacement demand from home sellers. Cities with recent easing may stay robust in 2Q, but growth in other cities has shown signs of rapid deceleration in the past few weeks. We lift our full-year total sales volume forecast by 3-4ppt to flat y-y in 2026, due in part to   a favorable base in 2H, and anticipate a LSD% decline in   2027. These forecasts will likely mean a continued, but soft, m-m home price downward trend during this period.

In our bear case, if homeowners, especially speculators, use the current rebound as an opportunity to dispose of their excess housing at an accelerated pace, secondary listing volume may reverse the YTD declining trend in a handful of high-tier cities, leading to more downside pressure on home prices despite the pickup in sales volume. This could in turn weaken resident sentiment again and result in faster deceleration in secondary sales volume, which may negatively feed back into home prices in a self-reinforcing downturn. In this scenario, we forecast secondary sales volume to be largely flat y-y and primary sales volume to drop 15-20% y-y for the full year, leading to an 8-10% y-y decline in total transaction volume in 2026.

Signposts to watch: We see May to August as a critical observation period, and suggest investors closely monitor visitation, secondary listing volumes/prices, transaction mix, and rental rates to confirm if an inflection is in the making. Should sales stay robust in the 2H, secondary home prices could turn positive m-m, but may take longer than before (vs. 3 and 9 months in Tier 1 and Tier 2 cities after sales volume rebounded in the 2014-15 recovery cycle, respectively), given the current less favorable macro, demographic, and housing market backdrop.

Adequate credit and policy achieves a normalized property market:  The central government aims to build a stable property market to support GDP growth but avoid a further property price rally. Recently, some local governments relaxed HPR, downpayment ratios and mortgage rates. Our base case factors in -3%, -3% and -5% yy growth in property prices from the end2025 level in tier 1, 2 and lower-tier cities, respectively.
